title: Use New Symbolic Elements
use_cases: Use when challenging traditional literary tropes or common metaphors to create unique atmosphere.
Implement when selecting alternative imagery and allegories that diverge from genre clichés.
Configure when balancing narrative originality with the maintenance of core reader expectations.
Use when evaluating if twists and subversions are effectively integrated or potentially alienating.
content:
Subvert common metaphors or symbols by avoiding them or using them in new ways. For example, rainy and dark days are usually seen as ominous. Perhaps an author writes rain only when there are happy scenes. Choose imagery and allegories that make sense for your story. A cozy mystery set in a bookstore can have a ferret instead of a cat. A fantasy can use magic through ham radios instead of fancy gadgets. Play with symbolism and symbolic elements to make things interesting.

I’m going to repeat myself here: it is still necessary for authors to follow or meet reader expectations most of the time—at least for the big, important ones. If you throw in a last-second twist that leaves the reader feeling duped, they’re not going to pick up your next book. Don’t take your subversions too far where readers see them as farcical or insincere. Do ensure you’re still being original in particular and intended ways.

If you want to know if your twists and turns are enough or too much, contact me today for help. As a comprehensive editor, I can work with you on subverting expectations through a brainstorming call, an outline critique, a manuscript evaluation, or a developmental edit. Let’s keep your readers on their toes by making your work truly original.
